topic: the concept of Newton's first law and seatbelts

easy.text: Why do passengers in a car lurch forward when the car suddenly stops?

options.text: Their bodies tend to keep moving forward due to inertia, even though the car has stopped
options.feedback: Correct -- this is a direct real-world example of Newton's first law (objects in motion tend to stay in motion unless acted upon).

options.text: The car pushes them forward on purpose
options.feedback: The car isn't pushing passengers forward -- it's the passenger's own inertia keeping them moving forward as the car stops.
Gravity's strength doesn't change during braking -- this forward motion is explained by inertia, not a change in gravity.

options.text: This has nothing to do with physics
options.feedback: This is actually a classic, direct demonstration of Newton's first law of motion (inertia).

medium.text: How does a seatbelt help protect a passenger during a sudden stop, based on Newton's first law?

options.text: The seatbelt applies a force to the passenger's body, helping to stop their forward motion along with the car, rather than letting inertia carry them forward uncontrollably
options.feedback: Correct -- without a seatbelt, a passenger's inertia would carry them forward into the dashboard or windshield; the seatbelt provides the necessary force to prevent this.

options.text: A seatbelt eliminates the passenger's inertia entirely
options.feedback: Inertia is a fundamental property of matter and can't be "eliminated" -- the seatbelt instead provides a controlled force to counteract the effects of that inertia.

options.text: A seatbelt has no real function related to physics
options.feedback: A seatbelt's protective function is directly and specifically explained by physics principles, particularly Newton's first law (inertia).

options.text: A seatbelt makes the passenger's body heavier
options.feedback: A seatbelt doesn't change a passenger's mass/weight -- it applies a restraining force to counteract their forward inertia during a sudden stop.

hard.text: Airbags are often used alongside seatbelts to further protect passengers. How does an airbag's function relate to the concept of impulse (force × time) in addition to Newton's first law?

options.text: The airbag extends the time over which the passenger's forward momentum is stopped, reducing the peak force experienced compared to an abrupt stop against a hard surface like the steering wheel
options.feedback: Correct -- this combines both concepts: inertia explains WHY the passenger keeps moving forward, while the impulse-momentum relationship explains HOW the airbag reduces injury by extending stopping time.

options.text: Airbags actually eliminate the effects of inertia completely
options.feedback: Inertia isn't eliminated -- the passenger's forward momentum still needs to be stopped; the airbag simply makes that stopping process gentler by extending the time involved.

options.text: Airbags have no connection to the concept of impulse at all
options.feedback: Airbags are actually a classic, direct real-world application of the impulse-momentum relationship in physics.

options.text: Airbags work by increasing the force experienced during a crash
options.feedback: Airbags specifically work to DECREASE the peak force experienced, by extending the time over which the passenger's momentum change occurs.

easy.hard: This effect reflects a moving object's natural tendency to continue in its state of motion unless something acts on it.
easy.medium: Passengers keep moving because of the same principle that keeps any moving object going unless something stops it.
easy.easy: Passengers keep moving forward because of inertia, the tendency to keep doing what you were already doing.

medium.hard: Consider what specifically provides the necessary counteracting force to actually change the passenger's forward momentum along with the car.
medium.medium: Something needs to actually apply a force to stop the passenger's forward motion along with the car -- that's the seatbelt's job.
medium.easy: The seatbelt provides the force needed to stop the passenger along with the car.

hard.hard: Since impulse (force × time) equals the momentum change, and that momentum change is fixed, extending the collision time via the airbag proportionally reduces the average force experienced.
hard.medium: By spreading out the stopping process over a bit more time, the airbag reduces how hard the stopping force hits the passenger at any one moment.
hard.easy: By spreading out the stopping process over more time, the airbag makes the stopping force less intense.
